items.title: AfroPari analyze les finales de l’US Open 2026: Sabalenka vs la future n°1 mondiale, Zverev vs l’espoir américain
items.description: Samedi, Sabalenka et Rybakina se disputent le titre dames; dimanche, Zverev et Shelton jouent le titre messieurs – avec un chèque record de 5,5 millions de dollars à la clé. Mais l'argent n'est pas le seul enjeu. Installe-toi confortablement : AfroPari décrypte le contexte historique des deux finales et évalue les chances de chacun. Finale dames : Sabalenka vs Rybakina Aryna Sabalenka dispute sa troisième finale consécutive à l'US Open et vise un troisième titre d'affilée. La dernière à réussir cet exploit était Serena Williams, en 2012-2014 — personne ne l'a fait depuis. Sabalenka arrive à cette finale avec une série de 20 victoires sur ce tournoi et un record qu'aucun joueur, homme ou femme, n'a jamais établi dans l'ère Open : huit finales de Grand Chelem consécutives sur dur. Selon Aryna, sa défaite face à Madison Keys en finale de l'Australian Open l'an dernier lui a appris à « faire abstraction du bruit » et vu sa série de victoires, le bruit est bel et bien resté en dehors du court. Elena Rybakina a, elle aussi, une belle histoire à raconter. C'est sa première finale à l'US Open et sa quatrième en Grand Chelem, mais quel que soit le résultat du match, elle deviendra dès lundi la nouvelle n°1 mondiale. Le head-to-head est de 10-7 en faveur de Sabalenka, mais à égalité parfaite en finale de Grand Chelem : 1-1. Rybakina a remporté leur dernière confrontation, en finale de l'Australian Open 2026, l'avantage de Sabalenka au classement général ne garantit donc rien. AfroPari s'attend aussi à une finale serrée: la cote est de 1.754 sur Sabalenka contre 2.246 sur Rybakina. Côté style, Aryna mise sur la puissance et une pression constante, Elena sur un service qui coupe parfois l'échange avant même qu'il commence. Ce ne sera sûrement pas ennuyeux ! Finale messieurs : Zverev vs Shelton Alexander Zverev a battu Karen Khachanov en trois sets (6-3, 7-6, 7-6) pour rejoindre sa troisième finale de Grand Chelem consécutive. Après son titre à Roland-Garros 2026, l'Allemand vise un deuxième Majeur et fait figure de favori. Pour Zverev, c'est aussi un retour sur la finale la plus douloureuse de sa carrière. En 2020, il menait 2 sets à 0 face à Dominic Thiem et servait pour le titre avant de tout perdre. Six ans plus tard, le revoilà en finale à New York, cette fois déjà auréolé d'un titre du Grand Chelem. Shelton, lui, écrit sa propre page d'histoire. items.title: Govt approves ‘extraordinary security allowance’ for police, civil service officers in 26 KP districts
items.description: PESHAWAR: The federal government has designated 26 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) as “terror-affected”, declaring that all Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS) and Police Service of Pakistan (PSP) officers posted therein are eligible for an ‘extraordinary law and order and security risk allowance’, effective from July 1 this year, it emerged on Saturday. According to a notification issued by the Establishment Division to the KP chief secretary and seen by Dawn , the allowance for 26 of the 35 districts will be 250 per cent of the running basic pay and paid retroactively. It read that the ‘KP Extraordinary Law, Order and Security Risk Allowance’ would be admissible to PAS and PSP officers posted in Peshawar, Khyber, Mardan, Charsadda, Nowshera, Mohmand, Kohat, Hangu, Karak, Kurram, Orakzai, Bannu, Lakki Marwat, North Waziristan, Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Upper and Lower South Waziristan, Swat, Buner, Shangla, Bajaur, Upper and Lower Dir, besides Upper and Lower Chitral. Citing an August 18 letter from the Establishment Division to the KP chief secretary, the notification stated that Swabi and the entirety of Hazara Division, comprising Abbottabad, Haripur, Mansehra, Battagram, Torghar, Kolai-Palas and the Upper and Lower Kohistan districts, were “excluded for the purpose of admissibility of subject allowance”. The federal government requested the KP government to proceed with payment of the allowance with effect from July 1, 2026. In the August letter seen by Dawn , the Establishment Division said the government approved the grant for PAS and PSP officers serving in the “seriously disturbed KP districts”, due to the law and order situation and the danger to officers and personnel. It added that the allowance would be admissible only to PAS and PSP officers in districts categorised as seriously disturbed, which would be identified by the Interior and Narcotics Control Division at the start of each financial year. “Establishment Division will notify the districts where this allowance will be admissible, on [an] annual basis, at the start of each financial year,” the letter read. “The allowance shall be discontinued upon transfer of the officers from the notified districts.” It further stated that the allowance would be provided during sanctioned leave of any kind, except extraordinary leave, and would not be available during suspension, appointment as an officer on special duty, or training of any kind. Furthermore, it would not be treated as part of emoluments for the purpose of calculating pension and gratuity, and the cost of the allowance would be borne by the federal government. KP has seen a rise in terrorist attacks over the past year. According to the Annual Security Report 2025 from the Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), KP recorded a significant surge in violence last year as “fatalities rose from 1,620 in 2024 to 2,331 in 2025”. Due to a resurgence of terrorism, especially in KP and Balochistan, where attacks often target security personnel and LEAs , the state has intensified counter-terrorism operations. According to monthly data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), mainland KP recorded 54 terrorist attacks last month, marking a 50 per cent increase compared to July. Meanwhile, the merged districts recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August, marking a 126pc increase.

items.title: Lil Durk acquitted in US murder-for-hire trial, faces fresh case
items.description: Grammy-winning American rapper Lil Durk has been acquitted of all charges in a federal murder for hire case in the United States, but he remains in custody ahead of another trial scheduled for October. The Chicago-born rapper, whose real name is Durk Devontay Banks, was accused of orchestrating the 2022 killing of Saviay’a Robinson, the cousin of rival rapper Quando Rondo, in Los Angeles. A jury returned its verdict on Friday after three days of deliberations, acquitting the 33-year-old of five felony charges, including murder for hire resulting in death and conspiracy. If convicted, he could have faced a life sentence. His defense lawyer, Drew Findling, said Banks was “thankful” following the verdict, while supporters cheered outside the Los Angeles courthouse. Prosecutors had alleged that Banks organized the attack as retaliation for the 2020 killing of rapper King Von, who was signed to Banks’ Only the Family, OTF, record label. The August 2022 attack occurred at a petrol station in Los Angeles, where a vehicle carrying Rondo, whose real name is Tyquian Bowman, was targeted in a shooting. Bowman escaped unharmed, but his cousin Robinson was killed. Prosecutors alleged that Banks had offered a bounty for anyone who killed Bowman, arguing that he was under pressure from social media to avenge King Von’s death. The case relied heavily on testimony from three cooperating witnesses who had reached plea agreements with prosecutors. Two co-defendants, Deandre “OTF Dede” Wilson and David “Browneyez” Lindsey, were also acquitted of the murder for hire charges but convicted of stalking and conspiracy to commit stalking. Although Banks was cleared in the murder for hire case, he remains in custody because of a separate case in which he is scheduled to face racketeering, murder, and firearms charges on October 5. First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli said prosecutors were disappointed with the verdict but would proceed with the second trial. Banks founded OTF in 2010 and has established himself as one of the leading figures in Chicago rap. He has released seven albums that reached the top five of the US Billboard chart since 2019. He won the 2024 Grammy Award for Best Melodic Rap Performance for “All My Life,” featuring J. Cole, and has received three other Grammy nominations. items.title: Again, two Nigerians killed in South Africa’s xenophobic crisis
items.description: The Federal Government has confirmed the killing of two Nigerians in separate incidents in South Africa, amid renewed concerns over attacks targeting foreigners in the country. Oluwafemi Adeniyi, spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, disclosed this in a statement issued on Friday, identifying the victims as Taiwo Fakunle and James Nwankwo. According to Adeniyi, Fakunle was murdered at his residence in Kensington, Johannesburg, on September 4, while Nwankwo was reportedly killed the following day during what the ministry described as “gruesome interrogation techniques” by officers of the South African Police Service (SAPS) in Somerset, Cape Town. The ministry called on South African authorities to conduct thorough and transparent investigations into the circumstances surrounding the deaths and ensure that those responsible are identified and brought to justice. It expressed particular concern over the alleged involvement of law enforcement officers in the death of Nwankwo, describing the reported interrogation methods as “unacceptable”. The latest deaths come two months after two other Nigerians were killed in South Africa amid renewed anti-migrant tensions. The ministry said the recurring incidents, including attacks and destruction of property targeting Nigerians and other African nationals, raise questions about the commitment of South African authorities to curbing attacks against foreigners. It also expressed concern over South Africa’s failure to sign a memorandum of understanding for the establishment of an early warning mechanism agreed upon during bilateral discussions between Nigeria and South Africa. The Federal Government said it was actively considering “other concrete measures” to secure South Africa’s cooperation after previous diplomatic efforts. According to the ministry, such measures could include taking the recurring waves of xenophobic and Afrophobic attacks against Nigerians and other Africans before the Authority of Heads of State and Government of ECOWAS and the Assembly of Heads of State and Government of the African Union. The development comes as the National Assembly on Friday suspended all legislative engagements with South Africa over the continued attacks against Nigerians. The ministry said the government remained committed to protecting the lives and interests of Nigerians in South Africa. items.title: S&P et Fitch maintiennent inchangée la notation de la Tunisie à «B-»
items.description: S&P et Fitch maintiennent inchangée la notation de la Tunisie à « B- » , tout en lui conservant une perspective «stable», le pays étant soutenu par les fonds des bailleurs de fonds et les prêts des banques centrales. Il est également importateur d’énergie et subit les répercussions de la guerre. Le soutien à la notation provient de facteurs extérieurs à l’économie elle-même. La Tunisie a remboursé une obligation en euros de 700 millions d’euros en juillet grâce à des prêts de sa propre banque centrale. Le pays est par ailleurs importateur d’énergie et subit les conséquences de la guerre au Moyen-Orient : une facture énergétique alourdie par la fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz, ce qui creuse les déficits courants et fait grimper les dépenses de subvention à un rythme que le gouvernement ne parvient pas à compenser. Selon Fitch, la guerre affecte la Tunisie par un canal unique : le prix des carburants importés. Le déficit budgétaire devrait se creuser pour atteindre 6,4 % du PIB cette année — contre une médiane de 3,3 % pour les États notés «B-» —, les subventions aux carburants représentant à elles seules 0,8 point de pourcentage de cette hausse. Fitch prévoit que le déficit s’aggraverait encore de 1,4 point de pourcentage si le cours du brut se maintenait à 87 dollars le baril jusqu’en 2028. Le déficit du compte courant s’élargit à 3,9 % du PIB avant de repasser sous la barre des 2,5 % en 2027-2028, sous l’hypothèse d’une baisse des prix du pétrole. Concernant les sources de financement : la Tunisie a remboursé en juillet son euro-obligation de 700 millions d’euros grâce à des prêts de la Banque centrale ; le volume de ces prêts devrait atteindre 11 milliards de dinars en 2026, contre 7 milliards en 2024. Les sorties nettes de financement extérieur devraient refluer à 1,4 % du PIB, après avoir atteint un niveau record de 3,6 % en 2024, et les réserves couvriront 3,3 mois de paiements extérieurs cette année pour atteindre 3,7 mois d’ici 2028 — un niveau qui reste toutefois inférieur à la médiane de 4,1 mois observée pour la catégorie «B» . items.title: Greening must be part of Ghana’s development, not an afterthought – Prof Naana Jane
items.description: Vice President Prof Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang has urged Ghana to make greening an integral part of urban development rather than treating it as an afterthought. She said the rapid growth of towns and cities must be matched with greater attention to trees, gardens and green spaces. “Greening should therefore not be something we consider after development; greening should be part of development itself,” she said. Speaking on Saturday at the opening of the 14th Ghana Garden and Flower Show, Prof Jane Naana said the recent floods should serve as a reminder of the consequences of neglecting the environment. She said the country must address the plastics and household waste choking drains and waterways while also creating greener communities. “That conversation must not end when the floodwaters recede. Keeping Ghana clean and making Ghana greener are part of the same responsibility,” she said. According to the Vice President, green spaces do more than improve the environment. They can also create demand for local skills and businesses. “Green spaces improve where we live and work, while creating demand for Ghanaian skills and businesses,” she said. She urged local authorities, developers and businesses to help create demand for green spaces, while Ghanaian producers are equipped to meet that demand and pursue export opportunities. Prof Jane Naana also highlighted the economic potential of horticulture, saying the sector has an entire economy built around its beauty. “Behind what we see are growers, skills, services, markets, and livelihoods,” she said. She called for greater support for enterprises in the sector to become sustainable businesses capable of creating jobs, supplying larger markets and competing beyond Ghana. The Vice President said this would require attention to the entire horticultural value chain, including transport, storage, quality standards, finance and access to markets. “Since we are serious about green business, we must pay attention to the entire chain, from production to finance, and how products reach the market,” she said. She said existing government programmes provide a foundation for expanding the sector. Under the Feed Ghana Programme, vegetables are among the priority crops, with opportunities for support in irrigation, improved inputs, greenhouse production, and better market access. She also pointed to the establishment of farmer service centres across the country, which are intended to bring services closer to producers, including export support, inputs, machinery, and market linkages. Prof Jane Naana said horticulture also presents opportunities for young people by combining agriculture, technology, creativity and enterprise. “The opportunity is not only to encourage young people to grow more, but also to help them to see the businesses they can build around their produce,” she said. She further urged stakeholders to strengthen quality standards, financing and market access to help Ghanaian horticultural businesses compete internationally. “Training institutions can develop the skills the sector needs. Financial institutions can support viable enterprises. The private sector can develop markets, and movements such as this one can continue bringing the industry together and making its possibilities visible,” she said. She said the question for the country should be how to make Ghana greener while creating businesses and livelihoods. “A greener Ghana begins with how we understand and care for the environment around us,” Prof Jane Naana said.

items.title: Côte d’Ivoire : L’opposant Justin Koné Katinan écroué pour « actes terroristes »
items.description: Le 4ᵉ vice-président du Parti des peuples africains-Côte d’Ivoire (PPA-CI), Justin Koné Katinan, a été placé sous mandat de dépôt et déféré à la Section antiterroriste du Tribunal d’Abidjan, a annoncé le procureur de la République dans un communiqué publié vendredi 11 septembre 2026. Selon le communiqué, cette procédure fait suite à une plainte déposée le 7 septembre par le Rassemblement des Houphouëtistes pour la démocratie et la paix (RHDP) auprès du procureur de la République près le Tribunal de première instance d’Abidjan. La plainte visait Justin Koné Katinan pour des faits présumés de diffamation, d’injure par le biais d’un système d’information et de diffusion de fausses nouvelles. Après l’audition de la partie civile, le responsable du PPA-CI a été entendu par les enquêteurs de la Préfecture de police. À l’issue de l’enquête sur ces faits, le procureur a demandé la transmission du procès-verbal en renseignement judiciaire, en vue de la saisine du Tribunal correctionnel. Parallèlement, le procureur dit avoir instruit les officiers de police judiciaire d’entendre Justin Koné Katinan sur sa participation présumée aux troubles survenus pendant la période électorale de 2025. À l’issue de son audition, il a été gardé à vue puis déféré à la Section antiterroriste du Tribunal d’Abidjan. Une information judiciaire a été ouverte à son encontre, avec mandat de dépôt, pour plusieurs chefs d’accusation. Le communiqué cite notamment des faits qualifiés d’actes terroristes, d’attentat contre l’autorité de l’État, de complot contre l’autorité de l’État, de participation à un mouvement insurrectionnel, d’atteinte à l’ordre public, d’apologie des crimes de meurtre, d’attroupement armé et non armé, ainsi que de participation et d’organisation d’une manifestation interdite ou non déclarée. Il lui est également reproché l’incendie volontaire de véhicules appartenant à autrui, commis à Abidjan et sur l’ensemble du territoire. Le procureur précise que ces faits sont prévus et réprimés par les articles 3, 8 et 10 de la loi n°2024-360 du 11 juin 2024 portant répression du terrorisme, ainsi que par plusieurs dispositions du Code pénal ivoirien. Le parquet rappelle, par ailleurs, qu’il avait indiqué dans un communiqué du 24 octobre 2025 que les violences commises durant la période électorale ne resteraient pas impunies et que leurs auteurs, complices et commanditaires seraient recherchés, interpellés et jugés conformément à la loi. items.title: The Year Great-White Sharks Took Over Maine
items.description: If you spend a lot of time in the ocean, it is hard not to think about sharks. I visit the beach near my home in southern Maine regularly with my family, and almost every night from spring to fall, I go surf fishing after dark. For a long time, I soothed my anxiety with statistics—in America, you are far more likely to be killed by a riding mower than a man-eating fish—and by reminding myself that, in all my years of beachgoing and striped-bass fishing, I’d never encountered a great white in the wild. But then, late one night a few weeks ago, I saw one. It was, as best as I could tell, a juvenile white, and the experience was wholly anticlimactic: A dark triangular fin appeared about 10 yards from where I was wading. It cruised the shallows at a 45-degree angle to the shoreline and seemed uninterested in me. I backpedaled out of the water. This would be the year that I finally spotted a shark. Maine’s great-white population has been growing for some time—the state had its first fatal shark attack in 2020—and this season, sightings have been unusually high. In July, beaches in Phippsburg were temporarily closed due to a shark sighting. Last month , Mile Beach, Half Mile Beach, East Beach, Wells Beach, and multiple Biddeford beaches were closed for the same reason. At one point, nearly a dozen sharks were reported at Pine Point Beach in a 48-hour period. Then, a longtime lifeguard at Scarborough Beach, Greg Wilfert, was dragged five or six feet underwater by a shark that grabbed his rescue torpedo. After the incident, Wilfert and his fellow lifeguards began monitoring the water with drones. He told me that they’ve seen as many as 15 great whites a day, which they chase off with Jet Skis. (Curious if they were exaggerating, I accompanied a drone-owning friend to check things out on a random afternoon: We saw four great whites in 30 minutes.) [ Read: The blockbuster that captured a growing American rift ] But if seemingly everyone agrees that more sharks have been around this season than in the past, even scientists are having a hard time pinning down what exactly is driving the spate of sightings, and what it means about the future of Maine’s beaches. Jérôme Pinti, a senior scientist at the Gulf of Maine Research Institute, attributed the rising number of great whites to a combination of factors: Climate change has expanded the species’ northern range; the effects of shark-conservation efforts begun in the 1990s are beginning to be felt; and, because the state is home to large biomasses of prey species including striped bass and seals, all the new great whites are finding ample food. Pinti also said, however, that ascertaining the true extent of the state’s white-shark increase is difficult without a formal stock assessment, which has yet to be done. He noted that the growing popularity of recreational drone use muddies the picture. “I believe we have more sharks,” Pinti told me. But also, “everybody and their brother has a drone right now. So if you have drones above the water all the time, you’re gonna see sharks a lot more.” Whether the rise in shark sightings is because of an actual increase in the number of sharks swimming in Maine waters, or because new technology simply makes the fish easier to spot, is an open question. Another open question is what, if anything, Mainers and those who visit the state’s beaches should now do differently. Ryan McDermott, a co-owner of the Black Point Surf Shop in Scarborough, told me that the sharks are making him and his fellow surfers choosier about when they go out. “It better be pretty good surf to get you out there when you know that there’s more than a handful of great whites just around the corner,” he said. I suggested that coastal Maine may soon become Cape Cod 2.0—another New England tourist destination that has had to negotiate its own rapidly expanding population of toothy ocean inhabitants. McDermott corrected me: “It’s already kinda happened.” [ Read: Inside the dangerous, secretive world of extreme fishing ] When I tracked down Wilfert, an affable 71-year-old who bears more than a passing resemblance to Dog the Bounty Hunter , he was still manning his lifeguard post, flanked by a pair of massive Newfoundland water-rescue dogs. He walked me down to the water’s edge and showed me the frayed rope of his yellow rescue torpedo. He told me that he didn’t see the shark that came after him—he felt it. He thought his buoy had gotten caught on a boat propeller, until the fish dived and started dragging him down. “I’ve been here 55 years,” he said, “and I’ve never seen a shark.” When I asked Wilfert whether he’d changed his habits, he said he was still swimming, though he confessed that he was not going out as far and had recently relied on drone shark spotters. As our conversation ended, a pair of elementary-school-age boys ran up to the perma-tanned Wilfert to ask him if he was the lifeguard who had been attacked. They, too, wanted to hear about the shark. In the emptier-than-usual parking lot, a stone’s throw from the beach smoothie shack, I walked past a stylish woman unloading beach chairs while her teenage kids impatiently snapped their gum. I stopped on the way to my own car, identified myself as a journalist, and asked whether she was worried about the recent surge of great whites. “Not worried and don’t care,” came the reply. “My husband is a lobsterman.”

items.title: Cormac McCarthy’s Midlife Crisis
items.description: To understand Cormac McCarthy’s midlife crisis, look at America’s landscape. The fierce writer of biblical prose spent most of his first four decades anchored to Tennessee, a child of Appalachia with a lilting drawl and a regional outlook. By the early 1970s, he had published three Faulknerian novels—none of which sold well—and was struggling to finish a fourth book that aimed to chronicle his hometown of Knoxville in the way James Joyce had written about Dublin. McCarthy’s pockets were empty and his second marriage was failing. His then-wife, Annie DeLisle, recalled that on New Year’s Eve 1973, the year he turned 40, he suddenly announced that it was time for a change. As a friend put it, “He just walked off and left everything except his boots and his typewriter.” Pointing his truck west on I-40, McCarthy started driving and spent time in Tucson; Santa Fe; and Juárez, Mexico, before settling in El Paso, where he began researching a new novel called Blood Meridian . Few life swerves are so productive. The book represented a fresh direction. Instead of another story set in the forests and shambling urban peripheries of Appalachia, Blood Meridian (1985) was an epic Western. It ambitiously set out to align the nation’s past with humankind’s age-old thirst for violence: Wolves cull one another, and so do people. From then on, the fearsome stakes of the West—territorial competition, crime, blood, death—defined McCarthy’s fiction and yielded his strongest work. His next five novels, including the best sellers All the Pretty Horses (1992) and No Country for Old Men (2005), used desert plains and bleak landscapes to unspool a grim pessimism, shocking readers with stark visions of depravity while preserving the slenderest candlelight of hope: a few good souls carrying the fire. It was as though Appalachia’s dense woods and city fringes had prevented him from seeing the page clearly. Out west, there is nothing but sky. In Cormac McCarthy: A Legacy Revisited , the first major biography of McCarthy, who died in 2023 , Tracy Daugherty depicts his western reorientation as a turning point in his life and work but also looks for continuity. “The desert can be anywhere,” he writes; “the soul’s site of testing”—McCarthy’s lifelong fixation—is not limited to any one place. Although his departure was hurried, the transition took time. McCarthy made laps back to Tennessee during the 1970s and finished his Knoxville novel, Suttree , from his new base. The book was finally published in 1979 and unfairly panned by one critic as a “limited use of an enormous talent.” As for Blood Meridian , although it promised wonders to come, McCarthy’s first Western started off as a cult classic and only later, in the 1990s, began to find success. [ Read: On the death of Cormac McCarthy ] Yet once cemented, the relocation was the fulcrum of McCarthy’s life. After the ’70s, he never again lived in Tennessee or made Appalachian culture his subject. He eventually came to be so closely associated with the dusty boots and bleached bones of the West that new readers may be surprised to learn that the first half of his life was spent elsewhere. So why did he leave Knoxville? Daugherty presents a combination of personal failures and artistic imperatives that chased and lured him, respectively. Daugherty’s fascinating biography, which reflects impressive research in the Cormac McCarthy Papers at Texas State University, is very well told and filled with astute judgments about McCarthy’s 12 novels. Although Daugherty declines to elevate one part of his oeuvre over the other, the lesson of the biography—and the work—is clear. The cultural South may have been McCarthy’s home, but the West was his muse. McCarthy’s father and namesake, Charles McCarthy Sr., represented urban order; he was set on taming the young Cormac’s backwoods waywardness. McCarthy later claimed that his father had beat him savagely during his childhood, afterward calmly sitting back down to finish his supper. Cormac’s artistically inclined mother helplessly watched the abuse. McCarthy Sr. worked as general counsel for the Tennessee Valley Authority, a New Deal agency that displaced tens of thousands of Appalachian families to make way for hydroelectric power. He did so with brisk pragmatism and a clean conscience, infuriating his son. Each man was baffled and hurt as the other rejected his outlook. The tension drives the early pages of Suttree : “The world is run by those willing to take the responsibility for the running of it,” the father in the novel tells his meandering boy. Siding with the evicted, McCarthy slept on the porch, explored the forests, and caroused with Knoxville’s degenerate class. “Like Shakespeare’s Prince Hal, he liked to go slumming—remaining, just slightly, apart,” Daugherty writes. McCarthy listened and gathered material for his novels as often as he participated in the outlaw revelry. Yet he was no angel: A night with John Sheddan, a local misfit and frequent confederate, could as easily find the two sleeping in a barn or confined to a jail cell for public intoxication as discussing Thomas Hobbes. McCarthy studied physics and engineering at the University of Tennessee but never earned his degree, and began to read Dostoyevsky, Melville, and Faulkner during an uneventful stretch of Air Force service in the 1950s. His first marriage, to Lee Holleman, ended in divorce. Family and friends offered few durable tethers to home, terrain that lacked lasting fictional appeal too. McCarthy’s early novels, beginning with The Orchard Keeper in 1965, chronicled the types of Appalachian outsiders and scofflaws he liked to run with. They proved off-putting company for readers. The books stood out as much for their desperate circumstances and ghastly subject matter (incest in Outer Dark , from 1968; necrophilia in Child of God five years later) as for their baroque prose and gothic settings. Suttree , the best of these novels and an excellent book, was nevertheless digressive and full of obscure, almost impenetrable writing (“rhomboid and volute shapes of limestone jutted all brindled with mud like great bones washed out”). Critics recognized a rare talent but also a voice struggling to break free of Faulkner’s influence. [ From the December 2025 issue: Thomas McGuane is the last of the literary outdoorsmen ] As his books misfired, McCarthy lived in an eccentric poverty that has become the stuff of legend. He cut his own hair and cooked canned food on hot plates. Working odd jobs (warehouse attendant in Chicago, garbageman in New Orleans), he recalled scraping by in “cellars on unemployment and welfare.” Without gainsaying these sacrifices, Daugherty calls out some exaggeration and myth building. Both DeLisle and Holleman contributed income; McCarthy’s Random House editor Albert Erskine helped him land fellowships and grants; and his parents, despite his strained relationship with his father, were a ready safety net. Still, between McCarthy’s failed marriages, family tensions, dead-end buddies, and dry artistic well, he had little to keep him in Tennessee as his 30s drew to a close. A western reinvention allowed McCarthy to continue exploring timeless, elemental themes in a setting that befitted their gravity. In the American imagination, a cowboy’s journey is fraught, and his last breaths are tragic; a hillbilly’s exploits are hapless, and his final moments are merely uncomfortable. We cry for our heroes but wince for our outcasts. McCarthy sensed the difference. For a flailing author, the West also held commercial promise. “I ended up in the Southwest because I knew that nobody had ever written about it,” McCarthy later said. “Besides Coca-Cola, the other thing that is universally known is cowboys and Indians.” Daugherty bristles at McCarthy’s dismissal of “decades of Southwestern literature”—by Leslie Marmon Silko, Katherine Anne Porter, N. Scott Momaday, and Larry McMurtry, to name just a few—yet the remark reveals a certain canniness: McCarthy cared more about selling books than his austere reputation suggests. It is not the only time Daugherty upends his subject’s ascetic image. In person, McCarthy was courtly and gregarious, a warm conversationalist who liked to sing. One striking scene has him dressed in a new cream suit, dancing into the night on an ocean liner as he twirls and spins his partners. B lood Meridian proved to be McCarthy’s best novel and a modern masterpiece. Its protagonist is notably a young man who flees Tennessee for the West. The book follows the Glanton gang of scalp hunters in the mid-19th century along the U.S.-Mexico border. In ominous, hyper-violent language, McCarthy displays a nihilism that situates humankind on the raw continuum of predator and prey, river and rock: “The men as they rode turned black in the sun from the blood on their clothes and their faces and then paled slowly in the rising dust until they assumed once more the color of the land through which they passed.” Like an ancient mystic, McCarthy foresaw the endless reenactment of a horrifying cycle of brutality without meaning or purpose, a cursed birthright. “It makes no difference what men think of war,” says his most fearsome character, Judge Holden. “War endures. As well ask men what they think of stone.” To Daugherty, Blood Meridian ’s clear-eyed view of American history was as amoral as realpolitik: “Politics as force.” The Border Trilogy followed—the best-selling All the Pretty Horses leading on to The Crossing (1994) and Cities of the Plain (1998)—adding accessible characters and love stories to at last attract sales and awards. McCarthy’s writing began to shed some of its most ornate flourishes, taking on a stripped-down veneer. (Many of his later books were conceived as screenplays.) Critiques of the works as lightweight fare from the oracular McCarthy overlooked their hidden depths. This arresting insight, for example, comes to the young cowboy John Grady Cole in All the Pretty Horses : “He thought the world’s heart beat at some terrible cost and that the world’s pain and its beauty moved in a relationship of diverging equity and that in this headlong deficit the blood of multitudes might ultimately be exacted for the vision of a single flower.” Daugherty views McCarthy’s evolution in the Westerns as the pairing of a mature style with a genre framework. A similar combination has produced some of the best American movies of the past generation, by filmmakers such as Kathryn Bigelow and the Coen brothers, who directed an Oscar-winning adaptation of No Country for Old Men . Although he started over, McCarthy could not escape the past. His celebrated 2006 novel, The Road —a sort of postapocalyptic Western—is built on a tender father-son relationship that both reflects McCarthy’s experience as a late-in-life parent and implicitly rejects his own father’s heavy hand. Daugherty quotes wrenching correspondence in which McCarthy and his father tried to reconcile as grown men. “There was and is a strong artistic streak in me that I inherited from my mother’s family and it has caused me a great deal of anguish in my life but an even greater joy,” McCarthy wrote. “I think this was always suspect to you.” Another relationship that echoed in his fiction was one that endured longer than his three marriages combined. McCarthy met Augusta Britt several years after moving out west; they became lovers when she was 17 and he was 43. They remained close for 47 years, but she protested the way he kept using her in his books, including in plotlines that seemed to mirror her life. “Well, baby, that’s what I do,” McCarthy replied. “I’m a writer.” McCarthy attempted a second reinvention, a turn toward science. By the late 2000s, he was spending much of his time at the Santa Fe Institute, a multidisciplinary research center, where he hobnobbed with physicists, favoring philosophical conversations over writing books. The year before he died, he published a final pair of related novels , The Passenger and Stella Maris , which had been in progress for years; one of the main characters is a mathematics prodigy with a mental illness. In startling new reporting, Daugherty contends that McCarthy’s literary agent assembled the hodgepodge of pages and made the decision to break the mess into two books; McCarthy’s friends told Daugherty they suspected that the ailing writer had not even read the finished product. The result was unconvincing characters, mashups of McCarthy’s many interests, strange psychiatric sessions, and a lack of cohesion. [ From the January/February 2023 issue: The incandescent wisdom of Cormac McCarthy ] Maybe we all have only one good pivot in us. Or perhaps it was just too late for McCarthy to change course again. Whatever the case, his turn west in the 1970s reveals not just a man escaping personal failures but a restless writer who sensed that a wide new horizon might require him to expand his vision if he was to find his voice and his audience. The small-town hustles and degradations of Tennessee were ultimately too provincial for such an epoch-spanning talent, which demanded plains, mountains, and an endless expanse of sky to bring out its full potential. After all, deep in the Appalachian woods, you can’t see the buzzards circling. This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Cormac McCarthy’s Midlife Crisis.”

items.title: ECG procurement is where politicians ‘milk’ the company – Ben Boakye
items.description: Executive Director of the Africa Centre for Energy Policy (ACEP), Ben Boakye, has accused politicians and politically connected individuals of benefiting from procurement practices at the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG). He argues that the utility’s financial challenges go beyond technical and commercial losses, with inefficiencies and alleged abuses in procurement also contributing significantly to its difficulties. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, September 12, during a discussion on the proposed private sector participation in ECG, Mr Boakye described the state-owned power distributor as part of what he called the “spoils of election”. “The fundamental truth around this is that ECG is an essential part of the spoils of election,” he said. “And that is where politicians milk. So when they appoint somebody to go manage it, that is where they share the business, they share the money.” Mr Boakye said some of what is classified as losses at ECG should instead be viewed as benefits accruing to individuals and businesses that take advantage of inefficiencies within the company. “What we consider as a loss, it’s actually a benefit to many people who are lined up to actually milk it. And that’s the bare truth,” he said. ECG procurement Explaining what he believes drives the alleged leakages, Mr Boakye identified procurement as a major area of concern, claiming that some items purchased by ECG cost significantly more than their market value. “I’ve said it on this studio many times. When you pick an item that is procured by ECG, if you get an item that you can buy for one cedi on the shelf, ECG will buy it an average of seven cedis,” he said. He attributed the alleged price differences to procurement practices, including sole sourcing. “And that’s because of procurement problems, sole sourcing, and I’ve seen people, private people, who have gone in; they will quote their price, and somebody in there will tell you to make it X amount before we give it to you,” he said. When asked whether the difference was intended to facilitate the sharing of benefits, Mr Boakye responded: “The benefit that has to be shared. Absolutely, yes.” He said such practices contribute to higher costs and inefficiencies within ECG, arguing that the company’s expenditure problems must receive as much attention as its technical and commercial losses. “So beyond what we technically would say are technical and commercial losses, the expenditure problems even within the business will not allow the company to be sustainable,” he said. Mr Boakye questioned why an item that costs one cedi on the open market would allegedly be procured by ECG for several times that amount. “Why is it that an item that will cost one Cedi would be procured by ECG for seven cedis? And that is not a problem,” he asked. Private sector participation Mr Boakye also questioned whether transferring ECG’s management to private operators would, by itself, resolve the problems confronting the company. He argued that the debate should not be reduced to whether ECG remains state-owned or is handed over to private managers, but should instead focus on addressing the practices that have allowed inefficiencies to persist. “All we care about is ownership. If that is central, then fix the problem that sustains the ownership,” he said. According to him, private companies already play significant roles in ECG’s operations, including revenue collection and the repair and maintenance of transformers and power lines. “And this whole thing about the private sector, who is managing ECG’s business today?” he asked. “There are businesses that are tied to the cash flow of ECG that are more liquid and more profitable than ECG entities are.” He alleged that some of these companies have become financially stronger than ECG because of the contracts they receive from the utility. “They are collecting revenue, they are the ones fixing transformers, they are the ones fixing lines, and they are richer than ECG itself, because they are the ones doing the contracting,” he said. Mr Boakye described the situation as a form of “chronic capitalism” operating around a state-owned company. “So technically, we are practising chronic capitalism that we feel is socialism because government owns the main company,” he said. He argued that private businesses, rather than the state, are among those benefiting from the inefficiencies that have persisted within ECG. “There are private businesses that are making billions because of the inefficiencies that we have actually cultivated over the years,” he said. Consumers bearing the cost Mr Boakye also rejected the suggestion that the financial burden of ECG’s challenges is borne primarily by government. He said consumers are already paying for the cost of inefficiencies through electricity tariffs and other charges within the power sector. “Already people are reeling under the tariffs,” he said. “But is it not expensive? When I’m paying a tariff, right, I’m paying a tariff. And after paying a tariff, you know how much we’re paying? On every litre of petrol you buy, you’re paying more than two cedis to support the power sector.” He questioned whether it was therefore accurate to suggest that government alone bears the cost of ECG’s financial difficulties. “Who is paying? Is it the government? Is it the minister? It’s the same people who are paying,” he said. Mr Boakye maintained that any meaningful reform of ECG must therefore go beyond questions of ownership and address procurement, expenditure and the broader network of interests surrounding the utility. “So I don’t know what the fuss really is, but the problem is that we need to be intentional and honest about the problems that we have in that space and be able to address them,” he said.

items.title: Worst DR Congo Ebola epidemic ever passes 7,000 cases
items.description: More than 7,000 Ebola cases have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s worst outbreak of the deadly disease ever, according to figures from the Congolese authorities. Thought to have been spreading under the radar for weeks, the DRC officially detected the latest outbreak in mid-May, with nearly 3,400 people killed in its 17th epidemic of the highly infectious virus. It began in the northeastern Ituri province before spreading to conflict-plagued, remote eastern and northern regions where armed groups have roamed for decades, the presence of the state is weak and health infrastructure is largely lacking. Earlier this week the disease was confirmed to have spread to a seventh province, South-Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic and Congo-Brazzaville. According to the latest figures from the Congolese authorities, 7,022 cases have been recorded since the beginning of the epidemic, of whom 3,398 have died and 1,671 people have recovered. Most of the recorded cases are in Ituri, where Ebola has been detected in schools in the days after the post-summer holiday return to classes, causing alarm among parents and health workers. “We are very worried because we don’t know which child comes from which family or what the health status of the members of that family is,” Angele Magani, mother of a schoolboy in Bunia, Ituri’s provincial capital, told AFP. “We are so scared, even though the school authorities reassure us about the health measures that have been put in place,” she added. Bunia school official Roger Mungimbo told AFP that “there is a mandatory hand-washing system with soap, and we have also done everything possible to have a maximum of 30 pupils per classroom,” “We regularly make the children aware that they must not touch each other, must not greet each other and must wash their hands regularly,” he added. Ebola, which has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the last 50 years, is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and can cause severe internal and external bleeding and organ failure. The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment currently. Several treatments and vaccines are being tested. The post Worst DR Congo Ebola epidemic ever passes 7,000 cases appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Akébou/ chefferie traditionnelle : Le chef de canton de Djon reconnu officiellement
items.description: Kougnohou, 12 sept. (ATOP) – Le chef du canton de Djon (commune Akébou 1), Togbui Atikla Kwaku Martin Assianko II, désigné par voie coutumière, a reçu son décret de reconnaissance officielle le 11 septembre dans la localité. La cérémonie a été présidée par le préfet de l’Akébou, Toyi Kokou qui a rappelé au nouveau dignitaire les obligations encadrant la chefferie traditionnelle au Togo. L’autorité a particulièrement insisté sur le devoir de loyauté envers l’administration publique. Il a exhorté le chef canton à faire preuve d’équité envers les vulnérables, à privilégier la conciliation et à préserver la cohésion sociale dans l’exercice de ses fonctions. Le préfet a également invité la population, les cadres et les ressortissants du canton à soutenir leur chef en vue du développement local. Le nouveau chef a salué les efforts du Président du Conseil, en faveur de la revalorisation de la chefferie traditionnelle et de la sauvegarde des us et coutumes. Il s’est engagé à œuvrer avec dévouement pour le bien-être de ses administrés, dans le strict respect des lois républicaines. L’impétrant a sollicité le concours de la communauté pour dynamiser les secteurs social, économique et agricole du canton. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence du secrétaire général du gouverneur de la région des Plateaux, Aimé Koffi Vidouté, des maires des communes Akébou 1 et 2, des parlementaires ainsi que de nombreuses autorités coutumières. ATOP/PM/KKT/HKM

items.title: IPPs’ contractual arrangements partly to blame for energy sector problems – TUC’s Dr Otoo
items.description: Deputy Secretary General of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), Dr Kwabena Nyarko Otoo, has attributed part of Ghana’s persistent energy-sector challenges to the contractual arrangements with Independent Power Producers (IPPs). Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile , Dr Otoo also questioned the decision by the government to rely on an assessment of the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG) conducted by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), particularly at a time when organised labour is opposed to proposals for private-sector participation in the company. He said he found it “difficult and strange” that government would ask the IMF to undertake an assessment of ECG, arguing that the Fund has consistently advocated reforms involving greater private-sector participation in state-owned entities. “I even find it difficult and strange that the Ghana government will ask IMF to do this, the IMF that wants to see all public state entities privatised,” he lamented. Dr Otoo said the concerns of organised labour were particularly important in assessing ECG because workers and their representatives have first-hand knowledge of the operational challenges facing the company. He questioned why the IMF assessment was conducted without consultations with ECG workers or the TUC. “The IMF is pushing for the privatisation of ECG and at a time when TUC and all organised labour groups are against it, you go and ask the IMF to do an assessment of ECG, and they did not even talk to the workers of ECG; they did not even talk to the TUC,” he said. Dr Otoo argued that discussions about the difficulties facing Ghana’s energy sector must go beyond ECG’s performance and examine the contractual framework governing power generation. He identified the structure of agreements with IPPs as one of the factors contributing to the sector’s financial challenges. “The IPP contractual arrangement is part of the problem we are facing in this country when it comes to the energy sector,” he said. The TUC and other organised labour groups have expressed opposition to privatisation, while the government has argued that reforms are necessary to address persistent inefficiencies and financial losses in the energy sector. For Dr Otoo, however, any assessment of ECG and proposed reforms should take into account the perspectives of workers and organised labour, as well as the wider contractual and financial arrangements that have shaped Ghana’s energy sector. He maintained that focusing solely on ECG risks overlooking other structural factors contributing to the sector’s difficulties, particularly the agreements with IPPs that have generated significant financial obligations for the state.

items.description: More than 7,000 Ebola cases have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s (DRC) worst outbreak of the deadly disease ever, according to figures from the Congolese authorities. Thought to have been spreading under the radar for weeks, the DRC officially detected the latest outbreak in mid-May, with nearly 3,400 people killed in its 17th epidemic of the highly infectious virus. A Congolese hygiene specialist at the Muthiri Adventist Hospital disinfects the facility, in the Mutiri quarter of Butembo, North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of Congo, September 10, 2026. —Reuters It began in the northeastern Ituri province before spreading to conflict-plagued, remote eastern and northern regions where armed groups have roamed for decades, the presence of the state is weak and health infrastructure is largely lacking. Earlier this week the disease was confirmed to have spread to a seventh province, South-Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic and Congo-Brazzaville. According to the latest figures from the Congolese authorities, 7,022 cases have been recorded since the beginning of the epidemic, of whom 3,398 have died and 1,671 people have recovered. Most of the recorded cases are in Ituri, where Ebola has been detected in schools in the days after the post-summer holiday return to classes, causing alarm among parents and health workers. “We are very worried because we don’t know which child comes from which family or what the health status of the members of that family is,” Angele Magani, mother of a schoolboy in Bunia, Ituri’s provincial capital, told AFP. “We are so scared, even though the school authorities reassure us about the health measures that have been put in place,” she added. Bunia school official Roger Mungimbo told AFP that “there is a mandatory hand-washing system with soap, and we have also done everything possible to have a maximum of 30 pupils per classroom. We regularly make the children aware that they must not touch each other, must not greet each other and must wash their hands regularly,” he added. A Congolese hygiene specialist at the Muthiri Adventist Hospital disinfects the facility, in the Mutiri quarter of Butembo, North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of Congo, September 10, 2026. —Reuters Ebola, which has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the last 50 years, is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and can cause severe internal and external bleeding and organ failure. The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment currently. Several treatments and vaccines are being tested.

items.title: Droit au développement : les inégalités persistent
items.description: Quarante ans après la reconnaissance du droit au développement, des millions d’enfants grandissent encore dans une précarité qui leur laisse peu de perspectives. Pour certains, l’espoir d’une vie meilleure passe par le départ, parfois au péril de leur vie, à la recherche d’une école, d’un emploi ou simplement d’une existence digne. Ces parcours sont le symptôme d’un monde où les progrès réalisés depuis 1986 restent profondément inégalement répartis, a souligné vendredi à Genève Awa Dabo, Haute-Commissaire adjointe des Nations Unies aux droits de l’homme, lors d’une table ronde consacrée au 40e anniversaire de la Déclaration sur le droit au développement à Genève. Évoquant notamment la situation dans son propre pays, la Gambie, elle a décrit des jeunes pour lesquels l’avenir ne se joue plus nécessairement à l’école, auprès de leur famille ou dans un emploi, mais parfois à bord d’une embarcation de fortune. Ils entreprennent ainsi des « voyages périlleux, souvent au péril de leur vie, loin de chez eux et de leurs proches, à la recherche d’opportunités », a-t-elle expliqué. Leur conviction est simple : rester chez eux ne leur permettra pas toujours de mener la vie qu’ils espèrent, « une vie normale et épanouissante ». Des progrès, mais pour qui ? Depuis l’adoption de la Déclaration en 1986, des progrès considérables ont pourtant été enregistrés. Les revenus ont augmenté dans de nombreuses régions, davantage d’enfants ont accès à l’éducation, les systèmes de santé se sont renforcés et l’accès aux services essentiels s’est amélioré. Mais ces avancées masquent une fracture persistante. « Les inégalités pèsent lourdement sur la vie de centaines de millions de personnes, anéantissent leurs espoirs et bafouent leurs droits », a averti Mme Dabo. Le troisième Rapport sur les inégalités mondiales du World Inequality Lab illustre l’ampleur du fossé. Selon ses données, les revenus annuels cumulés de la moitié de la population adulte mondiale — environ 2,8 milliards de personnes — sont comparables à ceux des 5 600 personnes les plus riches de la planète. « Cela correspond à peu près à la capacité d’accueil d’une salle de concert », a relevé la responsable onusienne. L’éducation, révélatrice des écarts Les inégalités sont particulièrement visibles dans l’investissement consacré à l’éducation. Les dépenses annuelles par enfant s’élèvent à environ 200 euros en Afrique subsaharienne, contre 7.400 euros en Europe et 9.000 euros en Amérique du Nord et en Océanie. Ces écarts compromettent directement les perspectives de développement et la capacité des jeunes générations à construire leur avenir. À l’approche de l’échéance de 2030, les Objectifs de développement durable (ODD) accusent d’ailleurs un retard préoccupant. Le déficit annuel de financement du développement dépasse 4 000 milliards de dollars. Seuls 36 % des cibles mesurables sont en bonne voie, tandis que 15 % ont régressé depuis 2015. L’endettement, les déséquilibres commerciaux et l’insuffisance des ressources publiques aggravent encore ces difficultés, alors que l’aide internationale au développement a chuté de près d’un quart cette année et que les dépenses militaires mondiales ont fortement augmenté. Pour le H CDH , ce constat impose de renforcer la coopération internationale, de mobiliser davantage de financements pour le développement et de placer les droits humains au cœur des politiques économiques. « Nous ne pouvons pas attendre encore quarante ans pour concrétiser le droit au développement », a conclu Awa Dabo. Source : ONU Info L’article Droit au développement : les inégalités persistent est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Like Benzema & as good as Haaland – Alonso on Joao Pedro
items.description: Xabi Alonso says Chelsea striker Joao Pedro is similar in style to his former Real Madrid team-mate Karim Benzema – and at a comparable level to Manchester City ‘s Erling Haaland. The Brazil international, 24, has scored twice and provided two assists in his first three games of the season – and was named the Premier League’s Player of the Month on Friday. It was the first time Joao Pedro has won the award as he finished ahead of team-mate Cole Palmer, who was Chelsea ‘s previous recipient in September 2024. When asked whether the forward could be compared to the prolific Haaland, who won last season’s Premier League Golden Boot with 27 goals, Blues boss Alonso said: “I would say yes. “If you count how many top strikers we have in the Premier League, I’m sure that Joao [Pedro] is there, Haaland for sure is there. So I would rate him that way.” Joao Pedro signed a new contract at Stamford Bridge last month to stay until 2034, and was handed Chelsea ‘s number nine shirt at the start of the season. He became the club’s first striker since Diego Costa to score 20 goals in a single season during his debut campaign and has struck 25 times and had 11 assists in 57 matches since joining last summer. In his last 57 matches for City, Norway’s Haaland has 42 goals and supplied nine assists. ‘He is still young, but many, many outstanding qualities’ Benzema won multiple Champions League titles and the Ballon d’Or while at Real Madrid Unlike Haaland, who is a specialist goalscorer, Joao Pedro has played as a midfielder, number 10 and winger during his career and possesses a more rounded skillset. Alonso, who made 195 appearances alongside former Ballon d’Or winner Benzema at Real Madrid, said there were also similarities between the Frenchman and Joao Pedro. “In many things he reminds me of Benzema, because he is good in the box, he is good out of the box, he is good coming to his left side, he is good with the head, he is very complete, he is intelligent,” added the Spaniard. “So yes, he is still young, still things to develop, but many, many absolutely outstanding qualities that he has.” Benzema, now 38 and a free agent, has scored 523 goals in 994 appearances for France, Lyon, Real Madrid and Saudi Arabian sides Al-Ittihad and Al-Hilal. Meanwhile, Joao Pedro was a surprise omission from Brazil’s squad for the World Cup this summer, but has since been recalled for September’s international fixtures against New Zealand and India. Asked whether the omission by Brazil manager Carlo Ancelotti, who coached Alonso at Real Madrid, had provided added motivation this season, the Chelsea boss said: “He had enough motivation. “He already had enough within him, so I didn’t need to go there. It was painful for him, but that is in the past. We are now focused on what he is doing well and what he can do better. “He has been outstanding. Not just in football terms, but in his personality, his maturity and his desire. He has a very clear goal this season, which is to have a great campaign and score a lot of goals.”

items.title: Le passeport tunisien se classe 120e mondial
items.description: Selon les données des Rapports sur les passeports , la Tunisie se classe au 11 e rang sur 54 pays africains, avec un accès total à 66 % des destinations du continent grâce à l’entrée sans visa, aux dispositifs d’entrée simplifiés ou à l’autorisation électronique de voyage. À l’échelle mondiale, le passeport tunisien occupe la 120 e place, avec un score de mobilité de 75 et un taux d’accès mondial de 37,9 %. Le score de mobilité de 75 se compose de 36 destinations accessibles sans visa, de 35 destinations relevant du visa à l’arrivée ou d’autres modalités d’entrée simplifiées, et de quatre destinations accessibles avec une autorisation électronique de voyage. Le rapport classe par ailleurs 123 destinations dans la catégorie où un visa est requis au préalable. L’Afrique, principale zone d’accès En Afrique, les titulaires d’un passeport tunisien disposent de 18 destinations sans visa, de 15 destinations avec visa à l’arrivée ou autre dispositif simplifié, et de deux destinations avec autorisation électronique de voyage. Dix-huit pays africains restent dans la catégorie du visa requis. L’accès total atteint ainsi 66 % du continent, un niveau nettement supérieur au taux d’accès mondial du passeport tunisien. Parmi les destinations africaines sans visa figurent notamment l’Algérie, le Maroc, l’Afrique du Sud, le Kenya, Maurice et le Sénégal. Le Burundi, Djibouti, l’Éthiopie, Madagascar, la Namibie, la Tanzanie et l’Ouganda apparaissent parmi les pays proposant un visa à l’arrivée ou une autre procédure simplifiée. Le Ghana et les Seychelles sont classés sous autorisation électronique de voyage, le rapport signalant pour les Seychelles un enregistrement touristique pouvant aller jusqu’à 90 jours. Des écarts marqués entre les régions En Asie, le taux d’accès atteint 48 %, avec huit destinations sans visa, 14 relevant de procédures d’entrée simplifiées et deux avec autorisation électronique de voyage. Le Japon est accessible sans visa pour 90 jours, tandis que la Malaisie est indiquée avec une carte d’arrivée et un séjour de 90 jours. Le Népal figure dans la catégorie d’entrée simplifiée avec une durée allant jusqu’à 150 jours, et l’Arménie jusqu’à 120 jours. En Europe, l’accès total n’est que de 2,1 % : la Turquie est la seule destination classée sans visa, pour 90 jours, tandis que 46 destinations européennes exigent un visa. Dans les six pays du Golfe recensés, toutes les destinations sont classées comme exigeant un visa, soit 0 % d’accès simplifié. Le taux d’accès atteint 35,3 % au Moyen-Orient, 42,9 % en Océanie, 43,8 % dans les Caraïbes, 33,3 % en Amérique du Sud, 26,1 % en Amérique du Nord et 40,0 % en Asie centrale. La Tunisie dans les classements comparatifs Au-delà de sa 11 e place en Afrique, la Tunisie se classe 8 e sur 24 pays dans le classement lié à la langue arabe et 8 e sur 22 au sein de la Ligue arabe. Elle occupe également le 18 e rang sur 57 pays de l’Organisation de la coopération islamique, le 11 e sur 54 au sein de l’Union africaine, le 68 e sur 132 dans le G77 et le 112 e sur 159 parmi les membres de l’Organisation mondiale du commerce. Dans le classement des pays les plus accueillants, qui mesure la facilité d’entrée en Tunisie pour les détenteurs de passeports étrangers et non la capacité du passeport tunisien à voyager à l’étranger, la Tunisie occupe la 83 e place sur 199. Le rapport présente aussi des signaux de réciprocité montrant que les conditions d’entrée peuvent différer selon le sens du voyage, sans attribuer ces écarts à une cause politique ou diplomatique. Réciprocité et conditions d’entrée en Tunisie Le rapport distingue l’accès des Tunisiens aux pays étrangers des conditions de visa pour entrer en Tunisie applicables aux titulaires de passeports étrangers. Dans les signaux de réciprocité, un premier groupe réunit des pays dont les ressortissants peuvent entrer en Tunisie sans visa, avec une autorisation électronique ou avec un visa à l’arrivée, alors que les Tunisiens doivent obtenir un visa pour s’y rendre. Un second groupe présente la situation inverse. Ces écarts sont rapportés comme des différences de régime d’entrée, sans jugement sur leur origine. Les durées de séjour soulignent également la diversité des conditions. La Barbade permet jusqu’à 180 jours sans visa, tandis que Fidji et le Vanuatu sont indiqués jusqu’à 120 jours. Le Japon, la Turquie et plusieurs autres destinations affichent des séjours allant jusqu’à 90 jours. Ces durées restent liées aux conditions spécifiques associées à chaque destination dans le rapport. Au total, le passeport tunisien obtient un score de mobilité de 75 grâce à 36 destinations sans visa, 35 destinations avec entrée simplifiée et quatre destinations avec autorisation électronique de voyage. L’Afrique demeure la zone offrant la couverture la plus large, avec 66,0 % d’accès, tandis que le classement mondial reste à la 120e place et que l’accès à l’ensemble des destinations mondiales s’établit à 37,9 %. Source : Rapports sur les passeports L’article Le passeport tunisien se classe 120e mondial est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Maroc : la croissance prévue à 4,2% en 2027
items.description: La croissance économique devrait s’établir à 4,2% en moyenne sur la période 2028-2029, selon rapport d'exécution budgétaire et de cadrage macroéconomique triennal accompagnant le projet de loi de finances (PLF) de 2027. Cette croissance serait soutenue par le dynamisme des activités non agricoles, dont la valeur ajoutée progresserait de 4,2% en moyenne par an, indique ce rapport publié sur le site du ministère de l'Économie et des Finances. Dans ce cadre, la valeur ajoutée du secteur secondaire augmenterait en moyenne de 4,3% par an, tandis que celle du secteur tertiaire enregistrerait une croissance annuelle moyenne de 4,1%. La valeur ajoutée agricole s’accroitrait, quant à elle, de 4,3% en moyenne sur la même période, sous l’hypothèse d’une production céréalière stabilisée à 70 millions de quintaux par an et de la poursuite du développement des autres filières agricoles. Ledit rapport fait également savoir que la préparation de la programmation budgétaire triennale (PBT) 2027-2029 s’inscrit dans un contexte national et international marqué par des défis économiques, sociaux et géostratégiques majeurs, face auxquels l’économie marocaine a fait preuve d’une résilience affirmée, portée par l’élan formateur engagé au cours de ces dernières années, et par la mise en œuvre soutenue de plusieurs chantiers structurants d’envergure. Ainsi, les prévisions de croissance nationale sont estimées à 5,3%, au titre de l’année en cours, et devraient maintenir la même tendance pour atteindre 4,2% au titre de l’année 2029, soutenue principalement par la bonne performance du secteur agricole et le maintien d’un dynamisme remarquable des activités non agricoles. Parallèlement, la maitrise de l’équilibre des finances publiques sur une trajectoire de réduction progressive du déficit budgétaire et du niveau d’endettement, s’inscrira au cœur de la programmation budgétaire en vue d’établir les marges budgétaires nécessaires au financement des différents chantiers, notamment en se fixant l'objectif de réduire le déficit budgétaire à 3% du produit intérieur brut (PIB) en 2027, 2028 et 2029, et le ratio d'endettement à 63% du PIB en 2029. Par ailleurs, les principales orientations pour la période 2027-2029 s’articulent autour de la maitrise des dépenses de personnel, de la rationalisation des dépenses de fonctionnement et de l’amélioration de l’efficacité des dépenses d’investissement. The post Maroc : la croissance prévue à 4,2% en 2027 appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Check out 41 countries Ghanaians can visit without a visa on ordinary passports
items.description: Ghanaian ordinary passport holders can travel to at least 41 countries across Africa, the Caribbean and other parts of the world under visa waiver arrangements, according to information from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The arrangements allow Ghanaian citizens to enter the listed countries without obtaining a visa in advance, although the permitted duration of stay varies in some cases. Most of the countries provide for stays of up to 90 days, while Grenada, Maldives and Zambia have shorter 30-day periods. Among the non-ECOWAS countries on the list are Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, The Bahamas, Dominica, Eswatini, Grenada, Guyana, Jamaica, Kenya, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Morocco, Maldives, Rwanda, Seychelles, South Africa, Singapore, São Tomé and Príncipe, Tanzania, Trinidad and Tobago, Uganda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Zimbabwe and Zambia. For Morocco, however, Ghanaian travellers are required to obtain a free Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) online before travelling. The United Arab Emirates is also listed, although the arrangement differs from a straightforward visa-free entry. Ghanaian citizens are required to obtain a visa from the UAE Embassy in Accra upon payment of the applicable fee. ECOWAS travel Ghanaian passport holders also enjoy visa-free access to fellow members of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), reflecting the regional bloc’s free movement arrangements. The countries include Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, Cabo Verde, The Gambia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone and Togo. Ghanaian travellers can generally stay in these ECOWAS countries for up to 90 days under the arrangements. Countries and permitted stay For the non-ECOWAS countries, the permitted periods are: Antigua and Barbuda – 90 days Barbados – 90 days The Bahamas – 90 days Dominica – 90 days Eswatini – 90 days Grenada – 30 days Guyana – 90 days Jamaica – 90 days Kenya – 90 days Saint Kitts and Nevis – 90 days Lesotho – 90 days Malawi – 90 days Mozambique – 90 days Morocco – 90 days, with a free ETA required Maldives – 30 days Mauritius – 90 days Rwanda – 90 days Seychelles – 90 days South Africa – 90 days Singapore – 90 days São Tomé and Príncipe – 90 days Tanzania – 90 days Trinidad and Tobago – 90 days Uganda – 90 days Saint Vincent and the Grenadines – 90 days Zimbabwe – 90 days Zambia – 30 days The information provides a useful guide for Ghanaian travellers planning holidays, business trips or other short visits abroad. Travellers are, however, advised to confirm entry requirements with the relevant embassy or immigration authority before departure, as visa waiver arrangements may be subject to conditions and can change.

items.title: FasoFoot : Le 9 Atlétic scelle un partenariat stratégique avec des sponsors qataris
items.description: Le 9 Atlétic, club burkinabè de Ligue 2, a officialisé une collaboration avec des investisseurs venus de Doha le vendredi 11 septembre 2026 à Ouagadougou. Ceux-ci ont livré un premier lot de matériel sportif et promettent un accompagnement technique et financier pour porter le club vers les sommets. C'est une étape importante dans la jeune histoire du 9 Atlétic. Le club burkinabè a matérialisé un partenariat avec des sponsors qataris, concrétisant des relations d'amitié et de fraternité nouées depuis plusieurs mois. La délégation, venue de Doha, n'est pas arrivée les mains vides. Maillots pour le staff et les joueurs, ballons, gadgets d'entraînement et bien d'autres équipements ont été remis au club. Signature de convention entre les deux parties Une dotation qui soulage immédiatement les finances d'une structure qui investit chaque année plusieurs millions pour équiper son effectif. Pour Ousmane Boly, fondateur du 9 Atlétic, ce rapprochement repose sur la réputation du travail accompli au Burkina Faso. « Ils ont entendu parler du sérieux du travail au Burkina. Ils ont également entendu parler des objectifs poursuivis par le 9 Atlétic », a-t-il expliqué. Selon lui, le football est aujourd'hui universel et les relations internationales contribuent à améliorer les performances d'un club. « Ils ont l'expertise technique, ils ont peut-être un peu plus de moyens que nous. L'un dans l'autre, en mettant ensemble nos efforts, on pourra faire grandir le 9 Atlétic, qui vise aussi à être un grand club au Burkina, pour ne pas dire un grand club africain ». Ousmane Boly donnant ses attentes de ce partenariat Le partenariat devrait avoir des effets concrets dès cette saison. Le club a déjà entamé son recrutement, mais l'appui technique et financier de ses nouveaux partenaires pourrait lui permettre d'attirer davantage de joueurs de qualité. Un renforcement qui, selon le fondateur, contribuera à élever le niveau de la Ligue 2 et pourrait permettre au club d'atteindre les sommets. Ousmane Boly a tenu à remercier ses homologues qataris, soulignant que ce type de dotation n'est pas donné à tous les clubs. « C'est déjà un don très important, qui soulage le club, qui va permettre de mettre du bon cœur aux joueurs et au staff technique. Je pense que c'est un très bon départ pour cette saison ». Une photo avec les nouveaux partenariats De son côté, Ilyas Saad Saoud, technicien algérien vivant au Qatar et membre de la délégation, a affiché la confiance de ses partenaires dans le potentiel burkinabè. « On croit aux talents du Burkina, et c'est pour cela qu'on a conclu ce contrat et ce partenariat pour tirer le football burkinabè au haut, et particulièrement le 9 Athletic Club », a-t-il conclu. En rappel, le 9 Atlétic est un club Burkinabè qui évolue en Ligue 2. Ils affichent ambition de monter en ligue 1 la saison 2026-2027. items.title: Présidentielle au Brésil : Flavio Bolsonaro visé par une enquête pour corruption et blanchiment
items.description: À moins d’un mois du premier tour de l’élection présidentielle brésilienne, la campagne de Flavio Bolsonaro est rattrapée par une nouvelle affaire judiciaire. Le sénateur de 45 ans, fils aîné de l’ancien président Jair Bolsonaro, fait désormais l’objet d’une enquête portant notamment sur des soupçons de corruption et de blanchiment d’argent. Candidat conservateur à la succession de Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Flavio Bolsonaro a réagi à l’annonce de cette procédure en affirmant n’avoir « rien à cacher ». Il a notamment défendu le financement du film consacré à son père, « Dark Horse », dont la production se trouve au cœur des investigations. L’enquête a été autorisée en juillet par le juge de la Cour suprême André Mendonça. Les autorités cherchent notamment à déterminer si des fonds provenant du banquier Daniel Vorcaro, actuellement détenu dans le cadre d’un vaste scandale financier, ont servi à financer des activités liées à la famille Bolsonaro. L’affaire concerne en particulier le financement de « Dark Horse », un biopic consacré à Jair Bolsonaro dans lequel l’acteur américain Jim Caviezel doit incarner l’ancien chef d’État. Flavio Bolsonaro avait reconnu en mai avoir sollicité et obtenu plusieurs millions de dollars pour financer le projet auprès de Daniel Vorcaro, patron de Banco Master. Le sénateur assure toutefois que cette opération relève d’un financement privé parfaitement légal. La justice cherche désormais à établir les véritables modalités de ces transactions et à déterminer si les sommes versées ont effectivement été utilisées pour la production du film ou si elles ont pu bénéficier à d’autres membres de la famille Bolsonaro. Selon des documents judiciaires consultés par l’AFP, Flavio Bolsonaro aurait rencontré personnellement Daniel Vorcaro à plusieurs reprises afin de discuter du financement. Les enquêteurs s'intéressent également à un transfert international de 12,3 millions de dollars effectué entre une entreprise indirectement liée au banquier et une autre structure associée à un avocat d’Eduardo Bolsonaro, le frère de Flavio installé aux États-Unis. La famille Bolsonaro à nouveau dans le viseur de la justice Cette enquête intervient dans un contexte particulièrement sensible pour la famille Bolsonaro. Jair Bolsonaro, président du Brésil de 2019 à 2022, a été condamné à 27 ans de prison pour son implication dans une tentative de coup d’État visant à empêcher le retour au pouvoir de Lula après l’élection de 2022. Il purge actuellement sa peine à domicile pour des raisons de santé. Son fils Eduardo Bolsonaro est également impliqué dans les procédures judiciaires liées à cette période. Installé aux États-Unis, il a été condamné au Brésil pour avoir exercé des pressions sur la justice dans le cadre du procès de son père. L’enquête visant Flavio ajoute ainsi une nouvelle dimension judiciaire à une campagne présidentielle déjà fortement marquée par l’affrontement entre le camp Bolsonaro et celui de Lula. Cette affaire intervient alors que Flavio Bolsonaro tente de s'imposer comme le principal candidat de la droite conservatrice face à Lula. Les deux hommes seraient au coude à coude dans certains sondages, dans la perspective d'un second tour qui pourrait avoir lieu le 25 octobre. The post Présidentielle au Brésil : Flavio Bolsonaro visé par une enquête pour corruption et blanchiment appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: I disrupted pre-season travel plans to prepare players – Arteta
items.description: Mikel Arteta says Arsenal were ready for their midweek Champions League flight delay – because he deliberately disrupted their training and travel plans in pre-season to prepare them. The Premier League champions were affected by air traffic control issues as they travelled to Italy to face Napoli on Wednesday. They eventually arrived three hours behind their schedule but manager Arteta said his team were ready because of his methods. “I love those challenges, I try to create them in pre-season,” Arteta said at his news conference on Friday, before Saturday’s Premier League trip to Sunderland (20:00 BST). “So when they happen, we have already experienced them and we are ready. “Get to the stadium very late, change the routine so the players have to do something else. When it happens, and it can – the flight can be cancelled, or the train is delayed, there is so much traffic, I don’t want the players and staff panicking. “When that happens, adapt to it. We have two or three hours on the plane – can we use it? Play together, spend some time together, sleep. “But don’t complain or use it as an excuse because it’s not helpful at all.” Arteta went on to add that his methods also include delaying meals or transport, take different routes to grounds and making the dressing room hotter and more uncomfortable for players. He said that it reduces the amount of stress and surprise on a matchday when such disruptions occur. It is not the first instance of Arteta using unusual methods in his team’s preparation. The Spaniard once brought a light bulb into the dressing room while asking his players to be energetic and shine. On another occasion, he even hired professional pickpockets to attend a team dinner to take phones and wallets from players, which was used as a lesson to teach them to stay alert. In 2023, he brought a dog named Win into the training ground to boost morale, saying that it was used to represent the team as a family. He is not opposed to others in the squad using his methods, either – in April, a fire was lit at the club’s training ground before they hosted Sporting in the Champions League.
